a: the land of the Chaldeans
p: The Chaldeans were tribes of southern Babylonia. Nebuchadnezzar's family came from them.
b: Kasdim (Akkadian Kaldu) were tribes of southern Babylonia whose dynasty held the throne from Nabopolassar (626 BC) to Nabonidus (a different line, 556-539). The Bible uses 'Chaldeans' for the Babylonians in general, and the Plain English Translation follows it. The heading names the city and the land. The Greek keeps only 'Babylon' here and lacks 'by Jeremiah the prophet' (Greek 27:1).

a: through Jeremiah the prophet
p: The headings say so. Many critical scholars think the poems are later.
b: Traditional view. The heading (50:1) and the closing note (51:64) give the poems to Jeremiah, and 51:59-64 shows him sending a scroll against Babylon in 594/593 BC. Critical view. Robert Carroll, William McKane and many others take the long poems as exilic or later, built from older lines (some repeated from Jeremiah 6 and 49) and from Isaiah 13-14, 21 and 47. Their reasons: Babylon is treated as about to fall, while Jeremiah elsewhere gives it seventy years (25:12; 29:10), and the style is a patchwork of earlier lines. Middle view. A core from Jeremiah, grown by later hands. Jack Lundbom defends much of the material as Jeremiah's. The text does not decide it.

a: Bel is put to shame; / Marduk is shattered
p: Two names for one god: the city god of Babylon.
b: Bel means 'Lord' and was a title of Marduk, patron of Babylon, whose temple Esagila stood in the city. Hebrew poetry names the one god twice in parallel lines. The Hebrew form Merodach is also in Merodach-baladan (Isaiah 39:1) and in Evil-merodach (52:31). In Isaiah 46:1 Bel and Nebo are carried away on pack animals, another picture of a defeated god. The Greek calls Marduk 'Maiodak' (Greek 27:2) and has no line about 'images' and 'idols' (see the variant).

a: Babylon is captured
p: The cry is repeated in Isaiah and in Revelation.
b: The announcement is in the past tense, as if the city has already fallen. The Hebrew perfect treats a certain future event as done (the 'prophetic perfect'). Isaiah 21:9 has the cry 'Fallen! Fallen is Babylon!', and Revelation 14:8 and Revelation 18:2 take it over for 'Babylon the Great'. For Jeremiah's hearers this was an act of faith: they lived under Babylon's rule.

a: a nation has come up against her from the north
t: The foe from the north turns on Babylon
p: In Jeremiah 'the north' meant Babylon. Now an army comes from the north against Babylon.
b: The book reads Babylon as Jeremiah's 'foe from the north' (1:14-15; 4:6; 6:22; 25:9), because armies reached Judah along the road from the north. Some scholars have thought the earliest of those oracles (chapters 4-6) pointed instead at Scythian raiders, whom Herodotus (1.105) describes sweeping through Asia in the 600s BC; the book itself does not name them. The same direction now marks the enemy of Babylon (50:9, 41; 51:48), and verses 41-43 use almost the same words as the oracle against Zion in 6:22-24. The reversal is the point: the judge is judged.

a: by a covenant for all time
t: The covenant that will not be forgotten
p: A lasting covenant is joined to the return from exile.
b: The phrase 'covenant for all time' (berit olam) recurs where Jeremiah and Ezekiel promise a new start after exile: Jeremiah 32:40 ('a covenant for all time'), Ezekiel 37:26 and Isaiah 55:3. Here the returning people themselves 'join themselves to the LORD'. Whether this is the new covenant of 31:31-34 is read two ways: Christian readers often say it is (compare Hebrews 8:8-12), and Jewish readers often take it as Israel's renewed commitment to the covenant of Sinai. The verse does not decide.

a: Their shepherds made them stray
p: The leaders led the people wrong.
b: A king or leader was a shepherd. Jeremiah has already said that the shepherds 'have not sought the LORD' (10:21) and that the LORD will gather the scattered flock (23:1-4). Ezekiel 34 develops the same picture at length. Verses 6-7 look back over Judah's history: lost sheep, shepherds who misled them, and enemies who ate them. Verse 17 adds that Assyria and Babylon were the lions.

a: Lost sheep, that is what my people have been.
p: The written text and the reading tradition differ in two small forms.
b: The Leningrad Codex marks two Ketiv/Qere pairs. The written text (Ketiv) has hayah, 'it has been', and shovevim; the reading tradition (Qere) has hayu, 'they have been', and shovevum, 'made them stray'. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere in both, which agrees with the plural 'sheep' and the plural 'shepherds'. The one Qumran copy of this verse, 4QJer-e, has the forms of the Ketiv (hayah, shovevim), as the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription gives them; the sense is the same either way.

a: We bear no guilt,
p: The nations said that Israel's sin made them innocent.
b: The enemies excuse themselves: Israel had sinned, so devouring it was no crime. Jeremiah 2:3 had said the opposite, that all who ate Israel's harvest would be held guilty. Both are true in this book: Babylon is the LORD's weapon (25:9; 27:6) and still answerable for its cruelty (50:17-18; 51:24, 35). The prophets refuse the idea that being used by God makes a nation innocent (Isaiah 10:5-19).

a: Run from the heart of Babylon!
p: Jeremiah told the exiles to settle in Babylon. Now they are told to leave when it falls.
b: In his letter Jeremiah told the exiles, in effect, to build houses and settle (29:5-7). The call here is for when the time comes: leave Babylon (50:8; 51:6, 45, 50). Isaiah 48:20 and Isaiah 52:11 have the same command, and Zechariah 2:6-7 repeats it for those still in Babylon after Cyrus. Revelation 18:4 uses it for a different Babylon. The 'billy goats that go out in front of the flock' picture the exiles leading the way home.

a: I am rousing a gathering of great nations
p: Cyrus's army was drawn from many nations.
b: The enemy is 'a gathering of great nations' (50:9), 'many kings' (50:41) and 'the kings of Media' (51:11). The oracle does not name Cyrus, but 51:11 and 51:27-28 name Media, Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz, and the Persian army was made of many peoples. Isaiah 13:2-5 also has a muster of nations against Babylon.

a: your mother will be put to deep shame
p: 'Your mother' is the city that bore its people.
b: A city can be pictured as the mother of her people, as in Isaiah 50:1 and Hosea 2:2. Here Babylon is the mother, and the looters of verse 11 are her children, so her shame is theirs. The last line, 'the hindmost of the nations', can also be read 'the least of the nations': Hebrew acharit is 'end' or 'rear'.

a: whistle at all her wounds
p: The same scorn once aimed at Judah now falls on Babylon.
b: The verb sharaq is a hiss or whistle of shocked scorn at a ruin. Jeremiah says it of Jerusalem (19:8), of Edom (49:17), and now of Babylon. The reversal is deliberate: what was said against Zion on the road to Babylon is said against Babylon on the road to Zion.

a: She has held out her hand
p: The gesture may mean surrender or a pledge.
b: The Hebrew says she 'has given her hand'. In Lamentations 5:6 'we gave the hand to Egypt and Assyria' means submitting or making a pact, and the sense here is probably surrender: Babylon yields. Others take it as a sign of begging for mercy. The next lines describe the walls falling.

a: This is the LORD's vengeance: / take your vengeance on her! / As she has done, do to her.
p: How can a call for vengeance be Scripture? Jews and Christians have answered in several ways.
b: Justice by measure. 'As she has done, do to her' (also 50:29; 51:24, 49) is repayment in kind (Exodus 21:23-25), applied to a nation that destroyed others. The vengeance is the LORD's own (51:56; Deuteronomy 32:35). The cry of the victims. Many readers hear the exiles speaking (51:35), alongside Psalm 137:8-9 and Lamentations, words given to the wronged so that they hand their rage to God and not to a mob. Christian limits. Romans 12:19 quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 against taking revenge, and Jesus commands love of enemies (Matthew 5:44). Christians differ on whether the prophets' calls for judgment are to be prayed or only read as God's declared justice.

a: her towers have tumbled
p: A word found only here.
b: Ashyoteyha occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain. 'Towers' is a guess from the parallel 'walls'; other proposals are 'props' or 'buttresses', that is, supports of the wall. The Greek has epalxeis, 'battlements' (Greek 27:15). The Ketiv spells the word differently from the Qere, which does not change the sense. In every case it names a part of the city's defenses.

a: now this last one, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, / has gnawed his bones
p: Assyria ate Israel, Babylon ate Judah. Both are called to account.
b: The lion picture counts two devourers. Assyria took the northern kingdom (722 BC, 2 Kings 17) and ravaged Judah; Babylon ended Judah. 'Gnawed his bones' uses a word found only here (itstsem), cracking the last of the body for the marrow. Verse 18 makes a promise of the comparison: Nineveh fell in 612 BC, and Babylon will be called to account in the same way.

a: he will graze on Carmel and in Bashan
p: Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim and Gilead were lands of the lost northern kingdom.
b: Carmel (the coast), Bashan (east of Galilee), the hills of Ephraim and Gilead were lands of the northern kingdom, taken by Assyria (2 Kings 15:29; 17:6). The oracle promises their return together with Judah (50:4, 33). The Book of Consolation has the same hope for Ephraim (31:5-9, 18-20), and Ezekiel 37:15-22 joins Judah and Joseph into one.

a: Israel's wrongdoing will be looked for
t: Guilt searched for and not found
p: Forgiveness is pictured as a search that finds nothing.
b: A court looks for the offense and finds none. It is the opposite of the search through Jerusalem in 5:1 for one honest person. The thought is that of 31:34 ('I will not remember their sin'), Micah 7:18-19 and Psalm 103:12. The ones forgiven are 'those I leave as a remnant'. Both Israel and Judah are named, as in 50:4.

a: Go up against the land of Merathaim
p: Two names with double meanings: places in southern Babylonia and words for rebellion and punishment.
b: Merathaim sounds like Hebrew 'double rebellion' (marah 'rebel'), and is probably the Akkadian mat marrati, the 'Bitter Land' by the Persian Gulf. Pekod is the Puqudu, an Aramean tribe east of the Tigris (Ezekiel 23:23), and sounds like paqad, 'call to account', the verb of verses 18, 27 and 31. The prophet plays with the names. The Greek translated them as words: 'go up bitterly against it' (Greek 27:21).

a: put them under the ban
p: The ban meant total devotion to destruction: no prisoners, no loot.
b: Cherem, 'under the ban', is the holy-war word for a place or people given over to God for destruction (Joshua 6:17-21). The prophets use it of foreign nations (Isaiah 34:2; Jeremiah 51:3). It says what the attackers are doing in the LORD's name. The history differs: Cyrus's army entered the city without wrecking it, so the oracle is not a plain forecast of how the fall would look (see 50:24).

a: How the hammer of all the earth
t: The hammer that is hacked off
p: The tool God used is broken in its turn.
b: Babylon was 'the hammer of all the earth'. In 51:20-23 the LORD himself calls a weapon 'a club' and shatters nations with it, and Babylon is both. Each picture says that Babylon's power was borrowed. Isaiah 10:15 asks whether the axe boasts over the one who swings it.

a: and you never knew it
p: Babylon was taken in October 539 BC with little fighting.
b: The Nabonidus Chronicle says that on the sixteenth of Tashritu (12 October 539 BC) the army of Ugbaru (Gobryas), Cyrus's general, took Babylon 'without battle', and that Cyrus himself entered on the third of Arahsamnu (29 October). Herodotus (1.191) says the outer parts were taken while those in the middle were at a festival and did not know it. Daniel 5:30 sets the end on the night of Belshazzar's feast. The Cyrus Cylinder claims Cyrus entered peacefully. The oracle's 'you never knew it' fits each account.

a: Cut down all her bullocks
p: Bulls stand for strong men and leaders.
b: In poetry bulls and rams are the strong ones, the nobles and captains (Psalm 22:12; Isaiah 34:6-7; Jeremiah 46:21; 48:15). Verse 27 addresses the attackers, and it says her best men are the ones to be struck down.

a: vengeance for his temple!
p: The burning of the temple is the crime named in the oracle.
b: The Babylonian army burned the LORD's house in 586 BC (52:13). This is the line the exiles waited for: 'vengeance for his temple' (also 51:11). The voice is that of fugitives from Babylon who are telling it in Zion, not of an army. Cyrus's own story is that Nabonidus had neglected the rites of Marduk's temple, so both sides spoke of a god wronged.

a: Look, I am coming at you, Insolence
p: Babylon is addressed by its sin.
b: The Hebrew is zadon, 'insolence', 'arrogance' or 'presumption', and the poem uses it as a name (50:31-32). The same root gives Edom's 'arrogant heart' in 49:16. The sin is not only cruelty. It is defying the LORD, 'the Holy One of Israel' (50:29).

a: Their redeemer is strong
p: God as the family's redeemer.
b: Go'el is the relative who buys back a relative who has sold land or himself (Leviticus 25:25, 47-49; Ruth 4). In Exodus 6:6 and Isaiah 41-54 God is Israel's redeemer. Here the redeemer 'will plead their case' (rib, a lawsuit), so he acts as relative, rescuer and lawyer. See also 51:36.

a: so that the earth may rest
p: One Hebrew word, two possible sizes.
b: Erets can be 'land' or 'earth'. If it is Israel's land, the line means that Judah gets rest. If it is the whole earth, Babylon's wars end for everyone. The Plain English Translation follows 'the earth' because Babylon is called 'the hammer of all the earth' (50:23) and the cup that made 'the whole earth' drunk (51:7).

a: on her officials and on her wise men
p: The wise men were Babylon's scribes, astrologers and omen readers.
b: Babylon's 'wise men' (chakamim) were the scholars who served the king by reading omens and the stars (Daniel 2:2, 12; Isaiah 47:12-13). Isaiah mocks them for being unable to foresee or stop the disaster. The sword strikes the thinkers as well as the fighters.

a: A sword on the babblers
p: A rare word. Old translations disagree.
b: Baddim occurs here and in Isaiah 44:25. It probably comes from bad, 'empty talk', used in Job 11:3 ('your babble'). The KJV has 'liars', the ASV 'boasters', and some modern translations 'diviners'. All of them fit a class of experts who talked big and said nothing true.

a: all the mixed crowd in her
p: The foreigners in Babylon, probably soldiers and workers.
b: Erev, 'mixed', names a crowd of mixed origin: those who left Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38), and the foreign allies and mercenaries of Jeremiah 25:20, 24. Babylon's empire used troops and workers from many conquered peoples. When they 'turn into women' they lose their courage; see 51:30.

a: A drought on her waters
p: The same three letters spell 'sword' and 'drought'.
b: The letters chrb are chereb, 'sword', or choreb, 'drought'. The verse follows three lines that begin 'A sword on...', so a reader might expect 'sword', but the Masoretic vowels give 'drought', which matches 'they will dry up' and 51:36 ('I will turn her sea to dry ground'). The KJV, ASV and the Plain English Translation follow it. Herodotus (1.191) and Xenophon (Cyropaedia 7.5) say Cyrus diverted the Euphrates so his men could enter by the river bed; the Nabonidus Chronicle does not mention it, and historians are divided on whether the story is true. Isaiah 44:27 and Revelation 16:12 also speak of the river drying up.

a: ostriches will make their home in her
p: The same animal list as Isaiah 13:21-22.
b: The Hebrew names desert creatures (tsiyyim), howlers (iyyim, perhaps hyenas or jackals) and 'daughters of the ostrich', the same creatures as Isaiah 13:21-22, the oracle against Babylon in Isaiah. Revelation 18:2 turns the picture into 'a home for demons'. Ruined cities are the haunt of wild things throughout the prophets (Isaiah 34:11-15; Jeremiah 9:11).

a: As when God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah
p: The overthrow of the cities of the plain is the model of total ruin.
b: This is the picture of Genesis 19:24-25, Deuteronomy 29:23, Isaiah 13:19 and Amos 4:11. The same words, with the same lines about no one living there, are spoken of Edom in Jeremiah 49:18. The Plain English Translation here keeps the English of Jeremiah 49:18 where the Hebrew is the same ('their neighbor towns', 'no human being'). Two differences stay because the Hebrew differs. Jeremiah 50:40 says 'God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah', as Isaiah 13:19 does, while 49:18 has the passive 'were overturned'. And 50:40 has ne'um YHWH, 'the LORD declares', where 49:18 has amar YHWH, 'the LORD says'; the English follows each formula.

a: Look, a people is coming from the north
p: Three verses are almost word for word the oracle against Jerusalem.
b: Verses 41-43 repeat 6:22-24 (the Plain English Translation keeps the same English where the Hebrew is the same), where the foe from the north comes against Daughter Zion. Here the army comes 'against you, Daughter Babylon', and it is the king of Babylon who hears the report and whose hands go limp. The one difference in verse 41 is in the Hebrew: 6:22 has me'erets tsafon, 'from a northern land', and a nation that 'is roused', while 50:41 has mitsafon, 'from the north', and adds 'many kings are roused'. The first great oracle of the book is turned on the power that carried it out. Scholars take this as deliberate reuse, whether by Jeremiah or by a later poet.

a: lined up like one man for battle
p: Two readings of one spelling.
b: The consonants spell ish, 'man', or esh, 'fire'. The Masoretic vowels give 'man', so the army is lined up 'like one man'. The Greek has 'like fire' (Greek 27:42). Either fits: a united army, or an army that burns everything.

a: and whoever is chosen, him I will set over it.
t: The lion from the Jordan, again
p: Verses 44-45 are the poem against Edom (49:19-20), reused for Babylon.
b: Verses 44-45 repeat 49:19-20, against Edom, and the Plain English Translation keeps the same English where the Hebrew is the same. The differences are the Hebrew's: 50:44 has 'I will make them run' (plural) where 49:19 has 'him', and 50:45 names Babylon and 'the land of the Chaldeans' where 49:20 names Edom and 'those who live in Teman'. 'Whoever is chosen' can mean the one the LORD picks to rule the conquered land, or 'the best of the flock'. The shepherd who cannot stand before the LORD is any ruler who would answer for the empire. Verse 46 has its own wording, not the Edom poem's (compare 49:21).

a: Leb-qamai
p: Leb-qamai is Chaldea written in a letter-swap cipher.
b: In the cipher called atbash the first letter of the alphabet is swapped for the last, the second for the next to last, and so on. Run through it, the Hebrew Kasdim ('Chaldeans') becomes Lev-qamai. Rashi says exactly this: 'Leb-qamai: Kasdim in the cipher At-bash'. The KJV did not see the cipher and translated the Hebrew words, 'the midst of them that rise up against me'. The Greek has 'Chaldeans' here (Greek 28:1). The same trick gives Sheshach for Babel in 51:41 and 25:26. Why a code is used here is unknown.

a: a destroying wind
p: The Hebrew word ruach means both.
b: Ruach is 'wind', 'breath' or 'spirit'. The Plain English Translation reads 'a destroying wind', the storm that winnows Babylon in the next verse. Rashi reads it as the spirit of the destroyer, the king of Persia and Media, whose spirit the LORD stirs up (compare 51:11). The Greek has a 'burning wind' (Greek 28:1). The line also echoes the wind of Jeremiah 4:11-12 sent against Judah.

a: The archer must not draw his bow;
t: Who is told not to draw the bow?
p: The verse is a known crux: some witnesses say 'Let the archer draw', others 'Let him not'.
b: The Masoretic Text says 'may not the archer bend his bow, and may he not rise in his coat of mail'. The Masoretes also mark a Ketiv/Qere: a second yidrokh, 'he bends', is read but not written. The Greek has the opposite sense, 'let the one bending bend his bow, and let him put on his armor' (Greek 28:3), and the JPS Tanakh (Gender-Sensitive Edition) also reads 'Let the archer draw his bow', with a footnote that some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions read 'Let not'. The Vulgate and the Targum agree with the Masoretic Text in the negative. Who is addressed? On the negative reading the archer and the soldier are Babylon's defenders, who are not even to be given the chance to fight, and the next line, 'Show her young men no pity', turns to the attackers. On the positive reading the whole verse is an order to the attackers: draw the bow, put on armor, spare no one. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text and puts the other reading in the variants.

a: but their land is full of guilt
t: Whose land is full of guilt?
p: The Hebrew says 'their land'. It could be Israel's or the Chaldeans'.
b: The Hebrew has 'their land'. The nearest people are Israel and Judah, whose land is full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel, yet they are not forsaken. The Plain English Translation follows that reading. Some translations take it of the Chaldeans' land, which makes the sentence a contrast between abandoned Babylon and Israel; the Greek reads 'their land was filled with injustice' (Greek 28:5), which is no clearer. The first reading fits the book's teaching that Judah's guilt was real and the LORD stayed faithful anyway.

a: Do not be silenced in her punishment.
p: The verb can come from two roots.
b: The verb tiddamu may come from damam, 'be silent', or from damah, 'be cut off, destroyed'. The Plain English Translation's 'be silenced' keeps the first and also fits the second, since to be cut off is to be silenced. The Greek has 'do not be cast away in her injustice' (Greek 28:6). The meaning is the same either way: do not be caught in her fall.

a: A cup of gold, that was Babylon, / in the hand of the LORD
p: In Jeremiah, Babylon is the cup God holds. In Revelation, the woman Babylon holds a cup.
b: God hands the nations a cup of wrath in Jeremiah 25:15-29 and Isaiah 51:17. Here Babylon itself is the cup, gold on the outside and poison within, and the LORD holds it. The nations drank, and 'act like madmen' (the verb is the one used of idol-mad Babylon in 50:38). Revelation 17:4 gives the woman called Babylon a gold cup 'full of disgusting things', and Revelation 14:8 and Revelation 18:3 say the nations drank her wine. See the chapter pages for how churches read this.

a: Bring balm for her wound
p: The balm that Gilead could not give Judah is offered to Babylon.
b: Jeremiah asked, 'Is there no balm in Gilead?' of his own broken people (8:22), and told Egypt to take balm in vain (46:11). Here the nations offer the same medicine to Babylon. In verse 9 the answer is that she cannot be healed. Whoever is speaking has given up treating her and decides to go home.

a: We gave Babylon treatment, / but she was not healed.
p: The speakers are not named.
b: Three readings: the foreign allies and subjects who tried to prop Babylon up and then leave (the 'let us go home, each to his own land' is then a call to the mixed crowd of 50:37); the exiles of Israel, who lived in Babylon, tried to be a good neighbor, as Jeremiah told them (29:7), and now are told to go; or a general voice of nations. 'Let us go home' and verse 10 ('recount in Zion') point to the exiles as the main speakers.

a: The LORD has brought out our righteous acts.
t: The LORD has brought out our righteous acts
p: The Hebrew word is plural and means the LORD's saving verdicts for Israel.
b: Tsidqot is the plural of tsedaqah. It means 'acts of righteousness' (Judges 5:11, 'the LORD's righteous acts'), 'vindications' or 'verdicts in our favor'. The line says that the fall of Babylon proves Israel's case against it. The Greek has 'the LORD has brought out his judgment' (Greek 28:10). The call is to 'recount' this in Zion, which is what 50:28 expects of the fugitives.

a: the kings of Media
p: The Medes helped destroy Assyria and then were absorbed by Persia.
b: Media (northwest Iran) joined Babylon in destroying Nineveh in 612 BC. About 550 BC Cyrus, king of Persia, defeated the Median king Astyages and took the Median empire, so the army that took Babylon in 539 was Persian with Median officers. Isaiah 13:17 also names the Medes. Daniel 5:31 speaks of 'Darius the Mede'. Rashi (on 51:1) speaks of 'the king of Persia and Media' together. The Greek has the singular 'the king of the Medes' here and in 51:28.

a: Fill the quivers!
p: The Hebrew word has two senses.
b: Shelatim are gold shields in 2 Samuel 8:7 and Song of Songs 4:4, and the word may also mean quivers. The Plain English Translation reads 'quivers' because the verb is 'fill', which suits an arrow case better than a shield, and because the Greek has 'fill the quivers' (Greek 28:11) and Rashi explains hashelatim as 'the quivers into which the arrows are placed'. Some translators read 'shields'. It makes little difference to the sense: the army is arming.

a: against the walls of Babylon
p: The walls were among the wonders of the ancient world.
b: Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt the city with a double wall, the Ishtar Gate (now in Berlin) and a canal and moat system fed by the Euphrates. Herodotus (1.178-181) describes walls of enormous height and breadth, figures that are probably inflated. The oracle's 'wide walls' (51:58) and 'high gates' are therefore real, not figures of speech.

a: You who dwell beside many waters,
p: Babylon sat among canals. Revelation 17:1 uses the same words.
b: Babylon lay on the Euphrates among canals and marshes. Revelation 17:1 calls the great prostitute the one 'who sits on many waters' and in 17:15 the waters are peoples. Jeremiah's own words, 'many waters', are the source. They give both the city's wealth and its weak point (51:32, 36).

a: the measure where you are cut off
p: The Hebrew line is hard.
b: The Hebrew amat betsa'ek is literally 'the cubit of your cutting off'. 'Cubit' is a measure; Plain English Translation 'the measure' says that the length of her time is run out. A second reading takes it as 'your thread of life' (a weaver's picture, from Isaiah 38:12), and Greek has 'into your belly' (Greek 28:13). The sense is clear: her time is over.

a: He made the earth with his power.
p: Verses 15-19 are repeated from chapter 10.
b: These five verses (51:15-19) repeat 10:12-16, a hymn to the Creator set against idols. In chapter 10 it follows a poem against the idols of the nations; here it follows the oracle against Babylon, whose gods are the idols. The two copies are nearly word for word. The reader is meant to see the first oracle of the book completed by the last.

a: because the image he casts is a lie,
p: Jeremiah's word for an idol is 'lie' (sheqer).
b: Sheqer, 'lie' or 'falsehood', is Jeremiah's key word for false prophets, false hopes and idols alike (10:14; 13:25; 23:25-26). An idol claims a presence it does not have, so it lies. 'There is no breath in them' contrasts the living God who made the world with a dead image that has no ruach.

a: They are empty breath, work worth mocking.
p: Hevel, 'breath' or 'vapor', is the word of Ecclesiastes.
b: Hevel is the word that begins Ecclesiastes ('vapor of vapors'). Jeremiah uses it of idols in 2:5 (those who followed worthless things became worthless) and in 10:15, which this verse repeats. 'Work worth mocking' can also be 'a work of deception', for the Hebrew word may mean either mockery or deceit.

a: Not like these is the one who is Jacob's share
p: The LORD is Israel's portion.
b: 'The share of Jacob' (cheleq Ya'aqov) recalls Deuteronomy 32:9, 'Jacob is his allotted share', and Psalm 16:5 where the LORD is the psalmist's 'portion'. The line is ambiguous in Hebrew: Jacob's share is the LORD, and the LORD's share is Jacob. The Plain English Translation keeps both, as Jeremiah 10:16 does. The one difference in the Hebrew is that 10:16 says 'and Israel is the tribe of his own inheritance', while 51:19 has no 'Israel' and no 'own' ('the tribe that is his inheritance'); the Plain English Translation follows each.

a: A club you are to me, / weapons of war.
p: The speaker is the LORD. The person addressed is not named.
b: The word mappets is found only here. Three readings: (1) Babylon was the club the LORD used on the nations (compare 50:23, 'the hammer of all the earth'), and now verse 24 repays her; (2) Cyrus and the Medes are the club in the LORD's hand against Babylon (compare Isaiah 45:1-4); (3) Israel is the club, as Micah 4:13 sees Zion thresh the nations. The Greek turns it into a charge: 'you scatter weapons of war for me' (Greek 28:20), a verb the Plain English Translation does not follow. Verse 24 turns at once to Babylon's repayment, which fits the first reading.

a: mountain of ruin
p: A mountain of power and a mountain of fire.
b: A mountain stands for a great kingdom (Daniel 2:35, 44-45). 'Mountain of ruin' (har hammashchit) says that the empire is a ruiner of the earth. 'A mountain of burning' pictures a burnt-out ruin, like a spent volcano. Some readers connect the high temple tower of Babylon, Etemenanki, with the tower of Babel in Genesis 11:1-9; the text does not say so. Verse 26 adds that no stone will be taken from her for a corner or a foundation, so her ruins will not even be quarried for building.

a: Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz
p: Three peoples from the north of Babylon.
b: Ararat is Urartu, the highland kingdom of the Lake Van region (Armenia). Minni is the Mannaeans, south of Lake Urmia. Ashkenaz is the Ishkuzai, usually identified with the Scythians (Genesis 10:3). Medieval Jews later used 'Ashkenaz' for Germany. All three were Babylon's northern neighbors and had been under Assyria and Media. The poem does not say they all fought at Babylon in 539.

a: Set nations apart as holy for war against her
p: 'Consecrate' is the word for preparing for a sacred battle.
b: The verb qiddeshu, 'set apart as holy', is used of preparing soldiers and nations for war (Jeremiah 6:4; Joel 3:9; Micah 3:5). In Isaiah 13:3 the LORD calls the invaders 'my holy ones'. War against Babylon is a sacred act because Babylon is judged.

a: Set an officer over the attack
p: The Hebrew word for 'officer' is an Akkadian word for a scribe.
b: Tiphsar is the Akkadian tupsarru, a scribe or official. It appears in the Bible only in Nahum 3:17 and here, as the title of a rank in the foreign army. The word shows the writers knew Babylonian titles.

a: they have turned into women
p: A figure of speech for losing courage.
b: To call a soldier a 'woman' was a way to say he was afraid. It is used of Babylon's foreign troops in Jeremiah 50:37, of Nineveh's soldiers in Nahum 3:13 and of the Egyptians in Isaiah 19:16. Verse 30 gives the reasons in order: they stopped fighting, they hid in strongholds, their strength was gone.

a: his city is taken from end to end
p: Herodotus tells the same story.
b: The Hebrew miqtsah can mean 'from the edge' (or from the far end) of the city. Herodotus (1.191) says that because of the size of Babylon the people in the middle did not know it had been taken at the edges, and were holding a festival. The Plain English Translation reads 'from end to end'. The picture of runners arriving one after another at the king fits a city too large to learn of its own fall at once.

a: Daughter Babylon is a threshing floor
t: The threshing floor and the harvest
p: Babylon is both the floor and the grain.
b: Threshing means treading or beating the harvest. Isaiah 21:10 calls the people 'my threshed one, my child of the threshing floor' in an oracle on Babylon, and Hosea 6:11 and Micah 4:12-13 use it of a nation judged. Revelation 14:14-20 combines grain harvest and grape harvest as judgment. Daughter Babylon is the floor while it is being stamped flat, and the harvest is her own people.

a: He has swallowed me like a sea monster
p: Nebuchadnezzar is pictured as a dragon from the deep.
b: Tannin is the sea monster of Canaanite and Israelite poetry, chaos that God defeats (Isaiah 27:1; 51:9; Psalm 74:13). Jeremiah gives it to the enemy: Nebuchadnezzar is the dragon who swallows and spits out. The picture is also one of eating: he has 'eaten' Zion, filled his belly, then 'rinsed out' the jar. The Greek has 'dragon' (Greek 28:34). The 'empty jar' echoes the smashed jar of Jeremiah 19.

a: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has eaten me up;
p: Five verbs in this verse have 'us' in the written text and 'me' in the reading tradition.
b: The written text (Ketiv) has 'us' on the five verbs of the verse (akhalanu, 'ate us'; hamamanu; hitsiganu; bela'anu; hedichanu), and the reading tradition (Qere) has 'me'. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, which agrees with the single speaker of verse 35, Zion. The Ketiv would make the whole people the speaker. The meaning is nearly the same.

a: May my blood be on the people of Chaldea!
p: Zion herself, and Jerusalem, speak as victims.
b: The speaker is Zion, personified. 'The wrong done to me and to my flesh' (chamasi u-she'eri) asks for a case against Babylon for violence; 'my blood' is like the blood of Abel that cries from the ground (Genesis 4:10) and the cry of Psalm 79:10. Revelation 6:10 has martyrs ask how long before God avenges their blood. In verse 36 the LORD answers: 'I am pleading your case.'

a: Look, I am pleading your case
p: God takes Zion's side in a lawsuit.
b: The Hebrew rib is a legal dispute. In Jeremiah 2:9 the LORD brings a case against Israel; here he takes up Israel's case against Babylon. Compare Micah 7:9 and Lamentations 3:58. The 'sea' and 'fountain' that he dries up are the Euphrates and its canals (see 50:38).

a: I will lay out their feast
t: A feast that ends in sleep
p: The drunken feast is the end of Babylon.
b: The LORD himself prepares the feast that ends in endless sleep, as he made Babylon a cup (51:7). The picture matches Isaiah 21:5, a table spread and sentries ordered to eat and drink, and Daniel 5, Belshazzar's banquet on the night Babylon fell. Whether the poet knew of a particular festival is not stated. Verse 57 repeats the 'endless sleep'.

a: Sheshach
p: A second cipher name for Babylon.
b: By atbash (see 51:1), the letters of Babel (B-B-L) become Sheshach (Sh-Sh-K). Rashi says: 'Sheshach: Babylon in the At-bash cipher' and cites the Midrash Tanchuma (Korach 12). The name occurs only here and in Jeremiah 25:26. The Greek lacks it in both places (Greek 28:41, and the end of Greek 32:12, which is Hebrew 25:26), which could mean that the translator's Hebrew did not have the cipher or that he left it out.

a: The sea has come up over Babylon
t: Marduk's sea turned on Babylon (Claude's theory)
p: In 51:34 Nebuchadnezzar is the sea monster. In 51:42 the sea buries Babylon.
b: Claude's theory. Babylon's national story, the Enuma Elish, tells how Marduk won his rule by killing the sea Tiamat and building the world from her body. Verse 34 makes the king of Babylon the sea monster, and verse 42 lets the sea cover the city. It may be a reversal of Babylon's own creation story: the god who drew order from the sea is overwhelmed by it. The poem does not say so, and the sea may simply be the flood of the invading armies (compare Isaiah 8:7-8). The Greek has the same line (Greek 28:42). Treat it as a suggestion.

a: I will pull out of his mouth what he gulped down.
p: The wealth and captives carried to Babylon's temples are taken back.
b: Bel (Marduk) is a god whose temple holds plunder. The vessels of the Jerusalem temple were put in the treasury of Nebuchadnezzar's god (Daniel 1:2; 2 Chronicles 36:7), and Ezra 1:7-8 says Cyrus brought them out and gave them back. The Cyrus Cylinder says he returned the gods of other peoples to their shrines. The 'Bel and the Dragon' story in the Additions to Daniel, which exists in Greek, later mocks Bel as a god who does not eat.

a: Come out of her, my people!
p: The command is repeated across the Prophets and then in Revelation.
b: Jeremiah has the command four times in this oracle (50:8; 51:6, 45, 50), and Isaiah 48:20 and Isaiah 52:11 and Zechariah 2:6-7 have it too. Revelation 18:4 says, "Come out of her, my people", of a later Babylon, so that those who hear it will not share in her sins. How many actually left, and when, is debated. Ezra 2:64-65 gives 42,360 for the assembly that returned, and scholars dispute how that figure fits the years under Cyrus. Jewish communities also stayed in Babylonia for centuries, and the Babylonian Talmud was made there.

a: violence in the land, ruler on ruler
p: The years before Cyrus were years of coups.
b: After Nebuchadnezzar died in 562 BC, his son Amel-Marduk (Evil-merodach) was murdered after two years, his killer Neriglissar died after four, and the young Labashi-Marduk was killed in a coup in 556 that brought Nabonidus to the throne. The Babylonian records, and Cyrus's rise next door, fit 'news in one year, and more news the next'. If the oracle comes from Jeremiah's own time (594), the line speaks of rumors and unrest in the empire at that time, which the Babylonian Chronicle notes for Nebuchadnezzar's tenth year.

a: will shout for joy over Babylon
p: Heaven and earth sing at a tyrant's fall.
b: Heaven and earth also sing when the LORD redeems Israel (Isaiah 44:23; 49:13) and when Babylon's king falls (Isaiah 14:7-8). Revelation 18:20 calls heaven, the saints and the prophets to 'rejoice over her'. It is a cosmic reversal of the earth's groaning under Babylon's violence (51:49).

a: as by Babylon's doing
p: The Hebrew can be taken three ways.
b: The Hebrew has 'Also Babylon [is] to fall, the slain of Israel; also for Babylon have fallen the slain of all the earth.' Readings: (1) Babylon must fall because of the slain of Israel, since by her doing the slain of the whole earth fell (the Plain English Translation); (2) Babylon must fall, and so must the slain of Israel, for the slain of all the earth fell at Babylon; (3) an address to the slain: 'Babylon must fall, you slain of Israel'. The Greek has only 'and in Babylon the wounded of all the earth will fall' (Greek 28:49).

a: outsiders have gone into / the holy places of the LORD's house
p: The Babylonians entered the temple, which Israelites were not to approach if unclean.
b: The temple's inner rooms were closed to everyone but the priests, and the outer court to non-Israelites. 'Outsiders' (zarim) walked into them in 586 BC. Lamentations 1:10 says the same, and Psalm 79:1 begins with the nations entering the LORD's inheritance. The shame is felt by the exiles who hear it.

a: Though Babylon should go up to the sky
p: Climbing to the sky is the sin of Babel.
b: Genesis 11:4 has a city and tower 'with its top in the sky'. Isaiah 14:13-14 has the king of Babylon say 'I will climb up above the heavens', and Obadiah 4 says the same of Edom. Even if Babylon fortified the sky, the destroyers come 'from me', the LORD.

a: a God of repayments
p: A rare title that sums up the oracle.
b: El gemulot, 'a God of repayments', is found only here. The root gamal means to give what is due, good or bad (Psalm 103:2, 'all his benefits'). Here it is the bad: Babylon is paid for what she did (50:29; 51:6, 24). The doubled verb ('he will surely repay') makes the repayment certain and complete.

a: declares the King
p: Babylon's king is nothing beside the LORD.
b: The signature is 'the King, the LORD of Armies'. The title answers the claim of the king of Babylon to rule the world. Jeremiah uses it elsewhere in the oracles against the nations (46:18; 48:15) and says the LORD is 'the everlasting King' (10:10).

a: So peoples labor for emptiness
p: Almost the same words are in Habakkuk's woes against Babylon.
b: Habakkuk 2:13 has almost the same saying about peoples laboring for fire and nations tiring themselves for nothing, in a woe against the city built with blood. Jeremiah's lines fit the same picture: the nations built Babylon's walls and her fire consumes them. The two prophets were contemporaries. Whether one quotes the other or both quote a proverb is not known. The Greek has a different ending (Greek 28:58).

a: in the fourth year of his reign
p: The date places Seraiah's journey in the year of the revolt rumors.
b: Zedekiah's fourth year was 594/593 BC. Chapters 27-28 are dated to the same year (27:1; 28:1) and say that envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon met in Jerusalem to plan revolt against Babylon. The Babylonian Chronicle records unrest in Babylonia in Nebuchadnezzar's tenth year (595/594) and a march to Syria in the eleventh. A trip to Babylon by Zedekiah or his envoy in this year would fit an effort to assure Nebuchadnezzar of Judah's loyalty. The scroll Seraiah carried foretold Babylon's fall, so the act was done quietly, away from Judah's politics.

a: Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah
p: Seraiah was Baruch's brother.
b: Baruch the scribe is 'son of Neriah son of Mahseiah' (32:12; 36:4; 45:1), so Seraiah was his brother. The family belonged to the court. This is not the priest Seraiah of 52:24, who was executed at Riblah, nor Seraiah son of Azriel (36:26).

a: Jeremiah had written in one scroll all the disaster that was coming on Babylon
p: The scroll Seraiah took was sunk in the Euphrates. What we read must be another copy.
b: The note says Jeremiah wrote 'all these words that are written concerning Babylon'. Readings: (1) The scroll contained the substance of 50-51, which Jeremiah or Baruch kept in a second copy; (2) the scroll was a shorter oracle that grew into 50-51, and the editor's 'these words' points to the final text; (3) the story was added to give 50-51 an origin in the prophet's day. In chapter 36 the burned scroll was written again, so a duplicate is natural in this book.

a: tie a stone on it and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates
p: The prophet's word is sunk with a stone, as the city will sink.
b: Jeremiah's sign-acts include the buried belt at the Euphrates (13:1-11) and the smashed jar (19:1-13). Here the act is done by another man, in Babylon itself. It works as a sealed promise: the words are read aloud, offered as a prayer to the LORD, and set going. Revelation 18:21 repeats the act when an angel throws a millstone into the sea and says Babylon will be thrown down the same way.

a: the words of Jeremiah
p: This note marks the end of the old collection of Jeremiah's words.
b: 'Up to this point are the words of Jeremiah' is a scribe's note of the kind found in Job 31:40 and Psalm 72:20. Chapter 52 is therefore placed outside 'the words of Jeremiah' and is taken almost word for word from 2 Kings. The Greek lacks the note and places chapter 52 right after the Babylon oracle.

a: daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah
p: Hamutal's father shares the prophet's name, but he is a different man.
b: The prophet Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth in Benjamin (1:1). Hamutal's father was from Libnah in the lowlands of Judah. Hamutal was also the mother of King Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:31), so Zedekiah was Jehoahaz's full brother. Jeremiah was a common name, and nothing in the text connects the two men.

a: until at last he flung them away from his face
p: Jeremiah's own warnings are echoed in the summary of the fall.
b: The verb hishlikh is the one in 7:15, where the LORD says he will fling Judah away from his face as he flung Ephraim. The same words appear in 2 Kings 24:20 and, of the northern kingdom, 2 Kings 17:20. Exile is pictured as being sent from his face.

a: Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
p: Zedekiah broke an oath of loyalty and counted on Egypt.
b: Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah king in 597 and changed his name to Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). Ezekiel 17:13-19 and 2 Chronicles 36:13 say Zedekiah swore an oath by God and broke it. Jeremiah warned against the revolt and against hope of Egypt (27:12-15; 37:5-10), and the Egyptian king Hophra (Apries) briefly drew the siege off (37:5). The Greek lacks verses 2-3 (see the variants).

a: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon arrived at Jerusalem
p: Jeremiah 39:1 gives the same date; Lachish and Azekah fall during the siege.
b: The tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year is 15 January 588 BC by the usual count, and Ezekiel 24:1-2 in Babylon dates the same day. While Jerusalem was under siege, the fortified towns of Judah fell one by one: Jeremiah 34:7 names Lachish and Azekah as the only ones left. The Lachish Letters, written in ink on pieces of broken pottery, include a captain's report that he watches for the fire-signals of Lachish 'for we cannot see Azekah'. Jeremiah bought a field at Anathoth during the siege (chapter 32) and was held in the guard court (37:21).

a: The city stayed under siege until King Zedekiah's eleventh year.
p: The siege was interrupted by an Egyptian army.
b: The siege began in the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year (January 588 BC, 52:4) and ended with the breach in the fourth month of his eleventh year (July 586 BC, 52:6), about thirty months. It was lifted for a while when an Egyptian army marched out (37:5, 11), and Zedekiah's government then took back the slaves it had freed (34:21-22). Famine became severe by the ninth of the fourth month (verse 6).

a: there he pronounced sentence on him
p: The Hebrew idiom is a court sentence on a rebel.
b: Hebrew says Nebuchadnezzar 'spoke judgments (mishpatim) with him'. The Plain English Translation gives the same English as 39:5, which has the same Hebrew. Jeremiah 1:16 uses the same expression for God's sentences. Riblah on the Orontes River in Hamath was a Babylonian base in Syria, where Pharaoh Neco had held Jehoahaz earlier (2 Kings 23:33). Zedekiah was tried as a vassal who broke his oath. 2 Kings 25:6 has the same idea, 'his case was judged', but its verb is plural, wayedabberu, 'they spoke', where Jeremiah 52:9 and 39:5 have the singular.

a: He also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah.
p: This sentence is in Jeremiah only.
b: 2 Kings 25:7 reports the death of Zedekiah's sons and not of the officials. Jeremiah 39:6 has both the sons and the nobles of Judah. The Greek has it here too. The officials would include men like those who demanded Jeremiah's death (38:4-6).

a: bound him in bronze fetters
p: Jeremiah told Zedekiah he would die in peace. Chapter 52 shows him blind in prison.
b: Jeremiah told Zedekiah that he would see Nebuchadnezzar and go to Babylon (32:4-5; 34:3), and if he obeyed he would 'die in peace' with the burning of spices as for his fathers (34:4-5). Chapter 52 gives a blinded man in a Babylonian prison. Readings: (1) the promise was conditional on surrender (38:17-18) and he did not obey; (2) 'in peace' means a natural death, not death by the sword, which the prison kept from him; (3) Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar kept him in prison until he died and buried him magnificently (Antiquities 10.154). Ezekiel 12:13 adds that he would not see Babylon. Josephus says Zedekiah did not believe either prophet because Jeremiah said the king of Babylon would carry him there while Ezekiel said he would not see Babylon (Antiquities 10.104-107). See 2 Kings 25:7.

a: On the tenth day of the fifth month
p: Kings and Jeremiah give different days.
b: 2 Kings 25:8 has the seventh day, Jeremiah the tenth, both in the nineteenth year. The Talmud harmonizes: the enemy entered on the seventh, the temple was set on fire on the ninth toward evening, and it burned through the tenth (Taanit 29a). The Jewish fast on the ninth of Av keeps this memory. A modern view is that the two reports come from different sources or that one date was changed in copying; no manuscript settles it, and the Greek of Jeremiah has the tenth.

a: He set the LORD's house on fire
p: The house that people trusted was burned, as Jeremiah warned.
b: Jeremiah had said in the temple gate that the house called by the LORD's name would become like Shiloh (7:12-14; 26:6), and that people must not say 'the temple of the LORD' as a charm (7:4). Psalm 74 and Psalm 79 and Lamentations 2:6-9 grieve this fire.  The Babylonian Chronicle for these years has not survived, so the burning is known only from the Bible and from the burnt layers found in Jerusalem.

a: whatever was left of the craftsmen
p: One Hebrew letter separates two words.
b: Jeremiah has ha-amon and 2 Kings 25:11 has ha-hamon, 'the crowd'. Amon is rare and is read as 'craftsman' (Proverbs 8:30 has a similar word). Some translators read it as 'crowd' (hamon), as Kings has. The Plain English Translation keeps each as the Hebrew has it. The Greek lacks the whole verse (see the variant).

a: to tend vines and to plow
p: Judah was not empty.
b: Jeremiah 39:10 says Nebuzaradan gave the poor who owned nothing 'vineyards and fields' at that time. Under Gedaliah at Mizpah the survivors gathered wine and summer fruit (40:10-12). The picture of a life on the land goes on for some time. Archaeology shows that Jerusalem and the Judean hills were hit hard while Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, suffered less. Whether the land was 'empty' is debated. Barstad argues for much continuity, and Lipschits for a heavy loss around Jerusalem with more continuity in Benjamin.

a: the bronze Sea in the LORD's house
p: Jeremiah had foretold the loss of the bronze objects.
b: Jeremiah 27:19-22 said the pillars, the Sea, the stands and the rest would go to Babylon, while Hananiah promised that the vessels already taken would be back within two years (28:3). The bronze never came back. Cyrus's gift of the gold and silver vessels is listed in Ezra 1:7-11. The pillars Jakin and Boaz and the Sea are described in 1 Kings 7:15-26. The Greek lacks verse 15 but has the vessel lists.

a: four fingers thick, and hollow
p: The numbers describe tall hollow bronze columns.
b: A cubit is about 18 inches, so a pillar of 18 cubits was about 27 feet, and its circumference of 12 cubits means a width of roughly 6 feet. Four fingers is about 3 inches, the thickness of the metal. 1 Kings 7:15-22 has the same dimensions and adds the lily work. 2 Chronicles 3:15 gives 35 cubits for the height, as does the Greek of Jeremiah (see the variant).

a: The capital of the one pillar rose five cubits
p: The same capital is given two heights in the Hebrew text.
b: Jeremiah and 1 Kings 7:16 say five cubits, 2 Kings 25:17 three. The numbers look like a copying difference in one of the three places. It is not known which was original, and the Greek of Jeremiah also reads five. The Plain English Translation gives each text as it stands.

a: Seraiah the head priest, Zephaniah the deputy priest
p: The priests named here are known from other books.
b: Seraiah was the grandson of Hilkiah (1 Chronicles 6:13-14) and the ancestor of Ezra (Ezra 7:1). Zephaniah son of Maaseiah is the priest to whom Jeremiah's opponents wrote letters from Babylon (29:25-29) and whom Zedekiah sent to ask for prayer (21:1; 37:3). Neither is the Seraiah of 51:59.

a: seven men of those who saw the king's face
p: The count differs from 2 Kings 25:19.
b: 2 Kings 25:19 says five, Jeremiah seven, and the Greek of Jeremiah also says seven. 'Those who saw the king's face' are the men who had direct access to the king (Esther 1:14). No manuscript decides whether five or seven is the older number, so each text is given as written.

a: 3,023 Judeans
p: This is the book's last use of Judeans (Jews).
b: Yehudim is 'Judeans' or 'Jews', the people of the kingdom of Judah. In Jeremiah it is found in stories of Gedaliah's time (40:11-12; 41:3), and in the reports of the deportations (here). In Nehemiah, Esther and later books it becomes the name of the people. The Greek lacks verses 28-30.

a: in the seventh year
t: Seventh or eighth? Eighteenth or nineteenth?
p: The year numbers here do not match 2 Kings or 52:12.
b: 52:28 puts the first exile in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, and 2 Kings 24:12 says Jehoiachin was taken in his eighth. The Babylonian Chronicle dates the capture of Jerusalem to the second of Adar in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year (16 March 597 BC), which agrees with Jeremiah's number. Likewise 52:29 puts a deportation 'from Jerusalem' in the eighteenth year, while 52:12 and 2 Kings 25:8 put the burning in the nineteenth, and Jeremiah 32:1 sets Zedekiah's tenth year in Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth. Scholars usually explain the differences in one of three ways: the books count the king's years differently (Babylon reckoned from the spring New Year and gave a new king an accession year; Judean scribes may have counted otherwise); the numbers describe different events (a deportation during the siege, before the spring that began year nineteen, as against the burning itself); or they come from different sources. No explanation is certain.

a: All the people came to 4,600.
p: The totals are far lower than in 2 Kings.
b: The three counts (3,023 + 832 + 745) add up to 4,600. 2 Kings 24:14 and 24:16 give 10,000 and 8,000 for the first exile alone. Readings of the low totals: Jeremiah counts only adult men, or only householders of Judah proper, and not the officers, craftsmen and their families; it gives only the deportations Nebuchadnezzar made with a registered count; the numbers in Kings are round and large. The three years are given in Nebuchadnezzar's reckoning (see the note on 52:28 for the year numbers): his seventh year is 598/597, the eighteenth 587/586, and the twenty-third 582/581. Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar invaded Syria, Ammon and Moab in his twenty-third year (Antiquities 10.181).

a: set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon
p: Clay tablets from Babylon list oil and barley for Jehoiachin.
b: Tablets found in Babylon and published by Ernst Weidner in 1939 list rations of oil and barley for many foreigners at the royal court, among them 'Ya'ukin, king of Yahudu' and five sons. One is dated to Nebuchadnezzar's thirteenth year (592 BC), so he was supported and called 'king' for years before the release in 52:31. The text of 52:32 does not name the 'kings who were with him'; the tablets show that Jehoiachin was one of many foreigners kept at the court. The Judeans in exile still dated by 'the exile of King Jehoiachin' (Ezekiel 1:2). Jeremiah 22:30 had said that none of his sons would sit on David's throne.

a: He changed out of his prison clothes
p: The story echoes Joseph in Pharaoh's prison.
b: The picture of a prisoner who changes his clothes, eats at the king's table and is lifted by a foreign king recalls Genesis 41:14 and 2 Samuel 9:7-13, where Mephibosheth eats at David's table. The same words end 2 Kings 25. Jeremiah ends here, with David's heir alive and fed in a foreign land.
